lesson.title: Counting Everyone: What a Census Really Requires
lesson.summary: A census is an attempt to collect data from every single member of a population rather than from a sample, and while it removes sampling variability in principle, it is often impractical, costly, or even less accurate than a well designed sample in practice.
lesson.body:
A census is a study that attempts to measure or survey every member of a population, rather than a subset of it. This stands in direct contrast to a sample, which examines only part of a population and then uses that part to draw conclusions about the whole. The most familiar example is the national census that many governments conduct, aiming to count and gather basic information about literally every resident of a country, but the term applies just as well to smaller settings, such as a teacher surveying every single student in a class of 28 rather than picking 10 of them.

The theoretical appeal of a census is straightforward: if data are gathered from every member of the population, there is no sampling variability at all, since there is no sample standing in for anything, only the population measuring itself directly. A population mean computed from a full census is the actual population parameter, not an estimate of it, so there is no margin of error to report in the way there would be for a sample statistic.

In practice, however, a full census is often difficult, expensive, or even impossible to carry out well, which is precisely why samples are used so often throughout this course. Consider a company that makes light bulbs and wants to know the average lifespan of bulbs from a production run of 50,000 units. A census would mean testing every single bulb until it burns out, which would destroy the entire product line in the process of measuring it, an approach that defeats the purpose entirely. Even in less extreme cases, a census of a large population, like every household in a country, is enormously expensive, takes a long time to complete, and in that time the population itself may change, since people are born, die, and move before the counting is finished.

A subtler point, and one that often surprises students, is that a census is not automatically more accurate than a well designed sample, even when it is logistically possible. Large censuses still suffer from nonresponse and undercoverage, the same sources of bias covered earlier, and because a census aims to reach everyone, it can be harder to follow up carefully with each hard-to-reach individual than it would be to follow up with the much smaller group of people missing from a well planned sample. National censuses are known to undercount certain groups, such as people experiencing homelessness or those wary of government contact, which introduces a real, systematic bias into supposedly complete counts.

The practical lesson is that the choice between a census and a sample is not simply about which one is more rigorous in principle; it is a tradeoff between cost, feasibility, timeliness, and the specific risks of bias each approach faces. For small, accessible populations, such as a single classroom or a small business's inventory, a census is often entirely reasonable. For large, spread out, or hard to fully enumerate populations, a carefully designed sample, especially a simple random sample, frequently delivers more trustworthy and far more timely information than an attempted census ever could.
